deep_analysis:
Quick Verdict

Unifi Home 100Mbps PrimePromo is a good fit for small households that mainly browse, stream, work from home and use several everyday devices. At RM89/month with three months of broadband charges waived, the price is attractive, but the 27-month commitment makes the contract more important than the headline promotion.

It is less compelling for households expecting significantly heavier usage during the next two years, particularly if you regularly download large files, run multiple high-bandwidth devices or want more headroom for future upgrades.


Cost & Contract Breakdown

The current Prime Promo price for the 100Mbps tier is RM89/month, with three months of broadband monthly charges waived. Unifi's campaign terms state a 24-month contract plus three additional months, making the commitment 27 months in total.

That means the three free months do not simply shorten the contract to 24 months. You remain committed for 27 months, while paying the RM89 subscription charge for 24 months.

Math Breakdown

Item / Calculation / Amount
Promotional monthly price—RM89/month
Contract period24 + 3 months27 months
Broadband waiver—3 months free
Paid months27 − 324 months
Total broadband subscription24 × RM89RM2,136
Effective cost over commitmentRM2,136 ÷ 27RM79.11/month

So, based purely on the promotional broadband subscription:

RM89 × 24 paid months = RM2,136

RM2,136 ÷ 27 months = RM79.11/month effective cost

The RM79.11 figure is an effective promotional rate, not the amount that will appear on every monthly bill.

Applicable taxes, optional add-ons and other charges should be checked separately before applying. The official campaign also specifies that the three-month waiver applies to broadband monthly charges and excludes add-ons.

What About Early Termination?

This is where the 27-month commitment matters.

Unifi's FAQ states that early termination during the contract period is subject to the standard early termination fee, based on the full subscription fees for the remaining months of the contract period.

The relevant Prime Promo package is RM89/month, so consumers should not automatically assume that an old RM99 RRP is the penalty basis.

For example, if 15 months remain, the simple subscription-fee calculation would be:

15 × RM89 = RM1,335

However, the final termination amount should always be confirmed against the customer's actual agreement and current Unifi terms before cancelling.


Performance & MCMC 90% Benchmark

Unifi advertises this package as up to 100Mbps download and 50Mbps upload.

For Fibre broadband, the commonly cited MCMC fixed-broadband MSQoS benchmark is more than 90% of the subscribed speed for at least 90% of the testing period. MCMC's fixed broadband network testing has used this threshold for fibre throughput.

For a 100Mbps plan:

100Mbps × 90% = 90Mbps

That gives a useful practical benchmark of approximately 90Mbps download.

But there is an important distinction:

A single Wi-Fi speed test below 90Mbps does not automatically prove an Unifi network fault.

MCMC-style network assessment and a customer's home Wi-Fi test are not the same thing. Your measured result can be affected by:

  1. Wi-Fi signal strength
  2. 2.4GHz interference
  3. Router placement
  4. Device Wi-Fi capability
  5. Ethernet cable quality
  6. Router port negotiation
  7. Other devices using bandwidth
  8. Test-server conditions

For a meaningful complaint about line performance, test using a wired connection directly through a suitable Ethernet port, repeat the test and eliminate other traffic first.

If properly conducted wired tests repeatedly show materially lower speeds, then it is reasonable to raise the issue with Unifi and request technical investigation.


Hardware & Technical Traps

The good news is that 100Mbps is not a demanding speed tier for modern networking equipment. The bigger issue is whether your existing equipment introduces an unnecessary bottleneck.

1. Cat5e is already enough

You do not need Cat6 simply because you subscribe to 100Mbps.

A properly functioning Cat5e Ethernet cable is sufficient for 100Mbps and Gigabit Ethernet.

Cat6 makes sense for new internal cabling or future-proofing, but replacing a perfectly good Cat5e cable will not turn a 100Mbps plan into a faster service.

2. Check the Ethernet port

If you want to test whether the fibre connection itself is delivering the advertised performance, use a device with a Gigabit Ethernet port.

An old 100Mbps-only Ethernet adapter can become the bottleneck and make troubleshooting unnecessarily confusing.

3. Wi-Fi 6 is included

The current Unifi coverage page lists the 100Mbps package with a Wi-Fi 6 Combo Box.

That hardware is more than adequate for a 100Mbps connection.

However, Wi-Fi 6 does not mean every connected device will achieve 100Mbps.

An older phone, laptop, smart TV or wireless adapter can still limit the connection.

4. Use 5GHz when speed matters

For devices located reasonably close to the router, the 5GHz Wi-Fi band is generally preferable when you want higher throughput.

2.4GHz has better range and wall penetration, but it is typically more congested and can produce lower real-world speeds.

If your router-to-device connection is weak, upgrading the broadband plan will not necessarily fix the problem.


Address-Level Reality

Do not confuse Unifi coverage with guaranteed installation at your specific unit.

Unifi's own coverage process tells customers to check their address and subsequently confirm port availability before proceeding with the application.

This matters particularly in Malaysian high-rise buildings.

An apartment may show Unifi coverage at the building or neighbourhood level while the actual unit still faces installation limitations because of available ports, building infrastructure or the existing access technology.

What About Old VDSL Buildings?

There is an important distinction between true FTTH and older copper-based broadband infrastructure.

TM has been progressively phasing out copper-based ADSL/VDSL broadband services as part of its network modernisation programme.

If you live in an older high-rise building and the service at your premises is still delivered through copper-based VDSL rather than FTTH, the access network—not your Wi-Fi 6 router—can become the limiting factor.

Do not assume that installing a newer router will solve a physical last-mile limitation.

For this reason, users in older apartments should confirm the actual access technology and installation feasibility at their unit, rather than relying solely on a general coverage result.


Who Should Get Unifi Home 100Mbps?

Good fit

  1. Small households
  2. 1–4 regular users
  3. Web browsing and social media
  4. HD video streaming
  5. Occasional 4K streaming
  6. Remote work and video meetings
  7. General home use across several devices
  8. Users prioritising a lower monthly broadband cost

Think about a faster plan if you:

  1. Frequently download very large files
  2. Have several people doing heavy downloads simultaneously
  3. Regularly run multiple high-bandwidth applications
  4. Have a large household with many active users
  5. Expect your broadband usage to grow substantially during the 27-month commitment

For gaming, remember that download speed is not the same as gaming performance. Latency, routing, packet loss and Wi-Fi stability can matter more than moving from 100Mbps to a much higher speed tier.


NetBijak’s Recommendation

The numbers make the PrimePromo attractive: RM2,136 in broadband subscription charges over a 27-month commitment, equivalent to RM79.11/month after accounting for the three free months.

The catch is the 27-month contract.

For a small household with moderate usage, 100Mbps is a practical entry-level fibre tier and the included Wi-Fi 6 hardware removes much of the need for additional networking equipment.

But don't choose it solely because the first three months are free.

Before applying, check these four things:

1. Confirm your exact unit is serviceable and has available port capacity.

2. Confirm whether the installation is genuine FTTH rather than an older copper-based access arrangement.

3. Test your existing devices and Ethernet hardware if you are upgrading from an older setup.

4. Read the early termination terms before signing the 27-month commitment.

This plan is worth considering for small households with moderate everyday usage. If you expect substantially heavier bandwidth demand during the next 27 months, compare the higher-speed tiers before committing.

The main value is the RM89 promotional price, three-month broadband waiver and included Wi-Fi 6 hardware. The main trade-off is the 27-month commitment, which reduces flexibility if your broadband requirements change.

The effective promotional subscription cost works out to RM79.11/month, before applicable taxes and additional charges.

Your home speed test measures the entire connection between the test device and the test server. The result can be affected by:

  3. Distance from the router

  6. Router placement

A Wi-Fi 6 router cannot remove a physical limitation in the last-mile connection.

Quick Verdict

Unifi Home 1Gbps is not simply about getting a higher speed number. At this tier, the bigger consideration is whether your home network can distribute gigabit bandwidth properly.

The RM249 1Gbps FTTR option is particularly different from a conventional router setup because it uses a Wi-Fi 6 Main Hub and Satellite Hub connected through fibre, designed to improve coverage across different rooms. Unifi lists the service at up to 1Gbps download and 500Mbps upload, with a 24-month contract.

That makes the plan more relevant to larger homes where the problem is not simply internet speed, but maintaining a strong connection away from the main router.

However, the hardware only solves part of the problem. Your phone, laptop, Ethernet adapter and other network equipment still need to support modern Wi-Fi or Gigabit Ethernet to take advantage of the connection.

Cost & Contract Breakdown

The current Unifi Home 1Gbps FTTR plan is listed at RM249/month, compared with an RRP of RM289, with a 24-month contract. It provides up to 1Gbps download and 500Mbps upload.

The FTTR package includes a Main Hub, Satellite Hub, splitter, access terminal box and optical cabling. Additional satellite hubs are available as paid add-ons, currently listed at RM850 one-time or RM40/month for 24 months per unit.

That matters because part of what you are paying for is whole-home network distribution, not just the 1Gbps fibre connection.

Performance & MCMC 90% Benchmark

Unifi specifies up to 1Gbps download and 500Mbps upload for the FTTR plan.

Using the commonly referenced 90% fixed-broadband throughput benchmark:

1,000Mbps × 90% = 900Mbps

So 900Mbps is the useful reference point when checking a gigabit fibre connection under controlled testing conditions.

For upload:

500Mbps × 90% = 450Mbps

A proper speed test should therefore be performed using a capable wired device where possible.

For the most meaningful test:

  1. Connect directly to the router using Gigabit Ethernet or faster.
  2. Use a Cat5e/Cat6 cable.
  3. Make sure the computer's network adapter supports Gigabit Ethernet.
  4. Stop other heavy network activity.
  5. Run several tests against reliable nearby test servers.

A Wi-Fi result should not automatically be treated as proof that the fibre connection is underperforming. Wireless performance depends on the client device, distance, interference and the radio environment inside the home.

Hardware & Technical Traps

At 1Gbps, the network equipment becomes much more important.

Gigabit Ethernet Is Essential

A device with only a 100Mbps Ethernet port cannot make full use of a 1Gbps connection.

The same applies to older switches, access points and adapters. The fibre connection can be delivering gigabit speeds while an individual device remains limited by the slowest component in its network path.

For wired connections, Gigabit Ethernet should therefore be considered the minimum.

Cat5e is normally sufficient for Gigabit Ethernet, so there is no automatic need to replace working home cabling simply because you upgraded to 1Gbps.

Wi-Fi 6 Helps, But It Does Not Guarantee 1Gbps

The FTTR package uses a Wi-Fi 6 Main Hub and Wi-Fi 6 Mesh Satellite Hub.

This is useful for distributing wireless connectivity around the home, but Wi-Fi 6 itself does not guarantee that a phone or laptop will record 900Mbps+.

Actual wireless speed depends on:

  1. Client device capability
  2. Number of spatial streams
  3. Channel conditions
  4. Distance from the access point
  5. Wall construction
  6. Interference from neighbouring networks

A Wi-Fi 6 router paired with an older Wi-Fi client can still produce much lower speeds.

FTTR Is About Coverage, Not Extra Internet Speed

This distinction is important.

The Satellite Hub does not turn 1Gbps into more than 1Gbps. Its purpose is to bring the network closer to areas where the main router would otherwise provide weaker wireless coverage.

The FTTR design uses internal fibre wiring to connect the equipment, and Unifi says the installation can be done without hacking through walls.

For a home with multiple rooms or difficult coverage areas, this can be more useful than simply buying a faster broadband plan.

1Gbps vs 500Mbps: What Are You Actually Paying For?

The jump from 500Mbps to 1Gbps is a 2× increase in download capacity, but that does not mean every online activity becomes twice as fast.

The difference is most obvious when transferring large amounts of data.

For example, downloading a very large game or transferring a large work file can benefit from the additional bandwidth if the remote server and local equipment can also sustain those speeds.

For normal web browsing, social media, video calls and standard streaming, the improvement may be difficult to notice.

This is why a 1Gbps plan should not automatically be considered a better choice simply because the advertised speed is higher.

Where the FTTR Setup Makes More Sense

The strongest reason to consider this particular 1Gbps package is the combination of gigabit bandwidth and distributed home networking.

It becomes more interesting when:

  1. The main router cannot provide consistent coverage throughout the house.
  2. Important rooms are far from the main router.
  3. You want wired-quality backhaul without relying entirely on wireless mesh links.
  4. Several parts of the house require stable high-speed Wi-Fi.
  5. Your main devices already support Wi-Fi 6 or Gigabit Ethernet.

This makes the FTTR component more relevant than simply looking at the 1Gbps number.

Address-Level Reality

The plan is still subject to TM infrastructure readiness and availability at the installation address. Unifi's FTTR terms also state that the service is provided on a best-effort basis and recommend compatible devices capable of supporting the bandwidth.

For landed properties, condominiums and older buildings, do not assume that an advertised 1Gbps plan automatically means the same installation setup is available at every unit.

Check the exact address before comparing plans based solely on the advertised speed.

Consider it if you:

  1. Need gigabit-class broadband for large data transfers.
  2. Have modern Wi-Fi 6 or Gigabit-capable devices.
  3. Have a larger home with difficult Wi-Fi coverage.
  4. Want fibre-based distribution between network points.
  5. Regularly upload large files or perform cloud backups.
  6. Already find 500Mbps sufficient but want more headroom for demanding transfers.

Consider 500Mbps instead if you:

  1. Mainly browse, stream and make video calls.
  2. Rarely download or upload very large files.
  3. Have older Wi-Fi devices.
  4. Do not have a coverage problem in your home.
  5. Would not use the additional gigabit capacity regularly.

For a larger property where Wi-Fi coverage is genuinely difficult, the FTTR architecture can therefore justify the higher-tier plan more convincingly than simply buying 1Gbps for everyday streaming.

But if your existing 500Mbps connection already meets your needs and your main limitation is not coverage or large data transfers, the additional monthly cost may not produce a noticeable improvement.

deep_analysis:
Quick Verdict

Unifi Home 2Gbps is different from a conventional 2Gbps single-device connection. Unifi describes the service as an Aggregated 2Gbps offering, with up to 2Gbps download and 1Gbps upload. The plan is priced at RM319/month with a 24-month contract and includes a certified Wi-Fi 6 Optical Network Router.

That “Aggregated” label is the most important detail to understand before subscribing.

A single device connected through a standard 1Gbps Ethernet port cannot simply pull the full 2Gbps. The benefit is better understood as more total bandwidth available across the home network, provided your router, wired equipment and connected devices can make use of it.

For most households, 1Gbps is already fast enough. The 2Gbps tier becomes more interesting when you have a genuine multi-gigabit networking setup or regularly move very large amounts of data.

Cost & Contract Breakdown

Unifi currently lists Home 2Gbps at RM319/month, with a 24-month contract. The plan provides up to 2Gbps download through an aggregated offering and up to 1Gbps upload.

There is no three-month free period attached to this basic 2Gbps plan.

Unifi's general FAQ states that there is no penalty for termination after the minimum contract period of 24 months. Early termination during the contract period is subject to the applicable terms and conditions.

At RM319/month, the 2Gbps plan carries a significant premium over 1Gbps. The extra cost therefore needs to be justified by actual network requirements rather than simply choosing the highest available speed.

Performance & MCMC 90% Benchmark

The headline specification is:

Download: Up to 2Gbps

Upload: Up to 1Gbps

Unifi specifically describes the 2Gbps download as an Aggregated offering.

Using the commonly referenced 90% fixed-broadband throughput benchmark:

2,000Mbps × 90% = 1,800Mbps

So 1.8Gbps is the useful 90% reference point when evaluating the connection under suitable testing conditions.

For upload:

1,000Mbps × 90% = 900Mbps

However, the aggregated nature of the service is important when interpreting the result. A speed test from one device with a 1Gbps Ethernet interface cannot demonstrate the full 2Gbps capability of the broadband service.

For a meaningful test:

  1. Use a device with a multi-Gigabit network interface where appropriate.
  2. Make sure the router and network equipment support the required throughput.
  3. Use suitable Ethernet cabling.
  4. Disable other heavy network activity during testing.
  5. Run multiple tests against reliable test servers.

A result below 2Gbps on a single 1GbE device does not by itself prove that the fibre connection is underperforming.

Hardware & Technical Traps

The hardware limitation is much more important at 2Gbps than at lower tiers.

1GbE Can Only Handle Around 1Gbps

A standard Gigabit Ethernet port cannot deliver 2Gbps to a single connected device.

This means a typical setup such as:

2Gbps Fibre → 1GbE Router Port → 1GbE PC

has a built-in limitation at the device connection.

The broadband line may have 2Gbps of aggregate capacity, but that particular device still has only a 1Gbps network path.

Multi-Gigabit Equipment Changes the Equation

To make better use of a 2Gbps connection, look for networking equipment with:

  1. 2.5GbE
  2. 5GbE
  3. 10GbE

This applies not only to the computer, but also to the router, switch, NAS and other equipment involved in the transfer.

For example:

2Gbps Fibre → Multi-Gig Router → 2.5GbE Switch → 2.5GbE PC

is much better suited to exploiting a multi-gigabit connection than a network built entirely around 1GbE.

Cat5e cabling can generally support 1GbE, but the cable alone does not determine the final speed. The ports and network adapters on both ends also need to support the required rate.

Wi-Fi 6 Is Not a 2Gbps Guarantee

The current basic 2Gbps package includes a certified Wi-Fi 6 Optical Network Router.

That does not mean a phone or laptop will receive 2Gbps over Wi-Fi.

Wireless throughput depends on the client device, channel conditions, signal strength, interference and other environmental factors.

If your main devices connect over Wi-Fi, the practical speed may therefore be considerably lower than the headline 2Gbps.

The Real Upgrade: 1Gbps Upload

The 1Gbps upload is arguably the more useful part of the specification for certain users.

At this level, large outbound transfers can become much less time-consuming.

It can benefit users who regularly:

  1. Upload large video projects
  2. Perform substantial cloud backups
  3. Synchronise large NAS libraries
  4. Transfer large datasets
  5. Move high-resolution media to remote storage
  6. Maintain workloads involving frequent large uploads

For a household that mainly consumes content rather than uploads it, the difference will be much less significant.

In other words, the value of 2Gbps is not only about downloading faster. The 1Gbps upstream capacity can be the more meaningful upgrade for data-heavy workflows.

Understanding Aggregated 2Gbps

This is the section consumers should pay particular attention to.

Aggregated 2Gbps does not mean every device automatically receives 2Gbps.

Think of it as a larger overall bandwidth pool.

For example, if several capable devices are transferring data at the same time, the connection can provide substantially more total capacity than a conventional 1Gbps connection.

But if your main computer has only a 1GbE port, that computer remains limited by its own network interface.

This is why a 2Gbps plan can make sense even when no single device consistently downloads at 2Gbps: the combined traffic across capable devices can make use of the additional capacity.

When 2Gbps Is Actually Useful

The strongest use case is not simply having more devices connected. It is having devices capable of generating and consuming large amounts of traffic at the same time.

Examples include:

  1. A workstation transferring large media files while another device performs a cloud backup.
  2. A NAS synchronising large datasets while other devices are downloading.
  3. Multiple multi-Gigabit wired devices transferring data simultaneously.
  4. A home network designed around 2.5GbE or faster connectivity.

If none of your devices exceed 1GbE and your upload requirements are modest, the additional capacity may remain largely unused.

Who Should Get Unifi Home 2Gbps?

Consider it if you:

  1. Already use 2.5GbE, 5GbE or 10GbE equipment.
  2. Regularly move very large files.
  3. Need up to 1Gbps upload capacity.
  4. Use a NAS or workstation for heavy data transfers.
  5. Frequently have several high-throughput devices active at once.
  6. Understand that the 2Gbps service is aggregated rather than a guaranteed 2Gbps connection to one 1GbE device.

Consider 1Gbps instead if you:

  1. Mainly use standard 1GbE equipment.
  2. Primarily browse, stream and make video calls.
  3. Rarely upload or download very large files.
  4. Have no practical multi-Gigabit networking requirement.
  5. Want to reduce your monthly broadband cost.

Address-Level Reality

The 2Gbps package is still subject to service availability at the installation address.

Unifi provides an address-based coverage check, so consumers should verify the exact property before assuming that the plan can be installed.

This matters especially for apartments, older buildings and properties where the available infrastructure may differ between locations.

Do not use general Unifi coverage in your neighbourhood as confirmation that the 2Gbps plan is available at your specific unit.

NetBijak’s Recommendation

At RM319/month, Unifi Home 2Gbps should be treated as a specialist upgrade rather than the automatic next step after 1Gbps.

Its biggest technical advantage is the combination of Aggregated 2Gbps download and 1Gbps upload. For users with multi-Gigabit networking equipment, large file-transfer requirements or substantial upstream workloads, that additional capacity can be genuinely useful.

For a typical home network built around 1GbE ports and ordinary Wi-Fi devices, however, the hardware can become the limiting factor before the broadband connection does.

The 24-month commitment also means this is not a plan to choose simply because “2Gbps sounds better”. At RM319 × 24 months, you are committing RM7,656 to the broadband subscription before applicable taxes and add-ons.

Before upgrading, check your router ports, switch ports, computer/NAS network adapters and actual upload requirements. If most of your network is still 1GbE, 1Gbps may already provide most of the performance you can practically use. If your network is genuinely multi-Gigabit, the 2Gbps tier becomes much easier to justify.
